b: Writer-director James Gray originally envisioned his latest work, Paper Tiger, as a sequel to his previous film, Armageddon Time. Both Queens-set stories from the 1980s sit squarely within the body of work of a filmmaker whose fascinations frequently return to his childhood milieu: the Eastern European and Jewish immigrant communities who settled in New York, many of whom brush up against the city’s seedy underbelly of organized crime.

But after grand-scale excursions to the far reaches of the Amazon jungle and outer space in 2016’s The Lost City of Z and 2019’s Ad Astra, respectively, something feels different about Gray’s recent homecoming. Like its forerunner, Paper Tiger pulls more openly from the artist’s own childhood experiences. The film’s inciting incident, in which striving working-class engineer Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) tangles with the Russian mob at the Gowanus Canal during a nighttime trip meant to impress his teenage sons, Scott (Gavin Goudey) and Ben (Roman Engel), comes directly from a formative experience in Gray’s own life. So, too, does the cancer diagnosis that Irwin’s wife, Hester (Scarlett Johansson), receives.

Gray’s assiduously classical style belies the thematic complexity and moral ambiguity of Paper Tiger, a stunning and sincere synthesis of personal storytelling and operatic tragedy. The Pearls’ struggle to get ahead in an increasingly cutthroat country—a struggle shared by Irwin’s brother, Gary (Adam Driver), an ex-cop trying to play both sides of a Russian mob scheme to cash in on the Gowanus Canal cleanup—mirrors the ruthlessness taking hold in Reagan’s America.

I spoke with Gray ahead of Paper Tiger’s theatrical release. Our conversation covered the film’s parallels to his prior work, how the story served as a vessel for his parental anxieties, and why he takes a hopeful view of the film’s conclusion despite the tragedies that befall its protagonist.

Paper Tiger feels in direct conversation with your previous work, both thematically and visually. If some of this is at least partly conscious, what do you gain from revisiting these elements with distance or additional experience?
Do you want the honest answer or the lie? I think you probably want the honest answer.

The honest answer is that often it’s conscious, for several reasons. One, I’m revisiting what is a nightmare in my mind because it had a vast impact on me. But here’s the other reason, and this is the honest part: I’m trying to make it better. I feel like I didn’t do it well enough the last time. I’m trying to make it mean more, be better, be more honest. It doesn’t mean I did; it doesn’t mean I do. But that’s part of the effect, really. I’m trying to get it more truthful and do it better to get at something deeper. Look, obviously, I’m not comparing myself to [Van Gogh], but it’s why when you go to the museum, you see all those Van Gogh self-portraits. He’s trying to get at a more honest view of himself. You feel the attempt over and over again. Honestly, I think because I feel like I failed last time, I’m trying to get it better.
Jean Renoir has that quote: “A director makes only one movie in his life. Then he breaks it up and makes it again.”

Did he say that? That’s an amazing quote. Well, I think it’s good to do that because there’s only one of you, and if the film is coming from you, how could it be otherwise? This is what you have to give to the world. This is what you’re expressing to the world, and I think it’s a good thing. There’s a great story of a session guy who came up to the guitarist Les Paul and said, “I’m really good at guitar, Mr. Les Paul.” He said, “Are you?” The guy [played], and it was technically amazing. Les Paul apparently responded and said, “That’s real good, fella. But when it plays on the radio, does your mama know it’s you?” Meaning, of course, that you have only yourself to express. Your personality must come through in your art, and if it does, that’s amazing.

In your recent master class at Locarno, you mentioned the idea that this obsession we have with newness and novelty is something given to us by capitalism, and that it isn’t intrinsic to art, which is about reminding us of what we already know. Is it possible we don’t see enough filmmakers doing variations of this kind because there’s a market force they’re responding to?

Here’s what I will say: I’m always a little bit leery when people say a work of art that they’ve just seen or read is “fresh.” Because what’s fresh today in my refrigerator is rancid tomorrow, and I don’t want something to be fresh. I want it to be enduring, an honest truth that I can keep revisiting. And also, what is freshness? I was watching the Powell and Pressburger movie A Canterbury Tale, and about three minutes in, you see a bird in the sky, and then it match-cuts to a plane 600 years later. Does that remind you of anything?
A little film by the name of 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Exactly right. The ape throws the bone, and it becomes a spaceship. You realize that Kubrick was not after something necessarily fresh, but he was after something bold. He was expressing himself directly to you about his fears of AI, which, of course, have weirdly become pretty prescient. Now, if something appears fresh, what people really mean is, “Boy, that feels like it’s the person speaking to me in a very direct way.” That has wonderful implications. What’s not wonderful is novelty just for the sake of novelty, without a connection to the broader idea of showing me who the person is who made it. Novelty is a trick.

Also, we forget that copyright is a fairly modern and totally corporate idea. Now, I think it has some great things. I don’t want people just stealing my stuff without asking me. But, by the same token, it does restrict our view, because stealing is what artists have done since the beginning of time. It’s all part of the soup. It’s a tough question you’re asking, and I don’t have a glib answer.

You’ve discussed Paper Tiger as starting out as a sequel to Armageddon Time, although you’ve changed the anchoring perspective from the children to the parents. What does that require of you differently as a storyteller and filmmaker?

I used my parents in this film as a metaphor for my and my wife’s experience raising our own children. As I’ve gotten older, I’ve noticed that I used to be on the side of the children. Now, I’m on the side of the parents. We try our best, but we’re going to make mistakes. The best we can do is to say, “You know what? We did our very best, but we really screwed up.” And hopefully, our children can say, “Yeah, you screwed up, but we forgive you.” Or they can be good enough to say, “Dad, you screwed up,” and I can be good enough to say, “You’re absolutely right. How do we fix it?” Sometimes, if it can’t be fixed, I can acknowledge that I did it and made the mistake. I used my own parents’ struggles as a way of investigating my and my wife’s struggle with what it means to be a good parent and spouse, to fight the fight, to be a decent person, and how the internal conflict that keeps us constantly at war with ourselves weighs on our souls.
One of your quotes that seems to be sticking from this press tour is “Art is not Sunday school.”
[laughs] I don’t remember saying that. That’s the part that scares me!

One of the reasons that turn of phrase stuck in my head is that the narrative format Paper Tiger and Armageddon Time most remind me of is the parable. Yet instead of neatly packaging a tidy lesson for the audience, you’re showcasing a moral complexity that contrasts with the simplicity of the human story.

What I think I meant by “Sunday school,” without remembering specifically the context in which I said it, is that our job is to point out things that are wrong. It’s not really our job to solve them. It’s not really our job to tell you our morally correct position. When you say “Sunday school,” what you’re really saying is a parable with a message at the end that tells you that the author of the parable or the lesson knows the correct thing to do. But that’s actually not what art’s supposed to do. Art is supposed to point it out, and then say, “What do we do?”

We have ambiguities here. We have complexities here. We have nuance here. And these will cause unending, durable difficulties. But you know what? I share those difficulties with you, and we will fight them together. It’s not my job to prove to you, Marshall, what a nice person I am or that I am on the correct side of history. No, no, because what is on the correct side of history today will not be on the correct side of history 20, 30, 50, 100 years from now. The moral and ethical landscapes are constantly in flux. We know that. So what can we do? The one thing we can do is say, “Boy, it’s hard to be a person. Let’s talk about the struggle. Let’s feel compassion for each other as we go through that struggle.” That’s all we have.

How did you see the role of irony playing into that artistic outlook in Paper Tiger? Irwin often has so little idea about the choices that are being made on his behalf that will come to define his life.
Well, let’s talk about this. It depends on what you mean by irony, a great term, because it has come to mean several different things in our culture. How do you mean it?

I meant it more in the sense of dramatic irony. Your films have a sincerity about them that’s so unique. We’re not above these characters, watching them like God and looking down on them in judgment. Yet by the end of this film, we have all this information about Irwin’s life that he doesn’t have yet. What’s stuck with me from Paper Tiger is this idea of how much of our lives are defined by forces we won’t learn about until it’s too late to change their course.

I think it reflects a broader idea about my own anxieties as a parent. One of the things that I’ve recognized now is that I’m in a constant state of worry much more than I used to be. It drives me a little bit nuts. There’s this app called Life360. Do you know what this app is?
Yes! My parents use it for my younger brother, but I managed to get out of the house just in time not to be surveilled by it.

I will look at this app on occasion. I’ll see my daughter with a little foot icon because she’s, like, walking down the street at two in the morning wherever she is in college, or my son will be on a bicycle in New York in the middle of traffic, which gives me a heart attack. I’m always in a constant low-level state of fear about what I don’t know, about what I can’t control, about how tenuous it all is, and how much love I still feel all the time for them, even if they’re out of the house. It has no place to go because they’re not home, and I can’t kiss them every night.

This idea that the narrative continues with a character who has large blocks of ignorance, because he doesn’t know all this stuff yet—that’s life! All these things will happen that we don’t know about yet, and it’s why we feel this anxiety and fear. How do we conquer that? It’s one of the enduring anguishes of our lives. Maybe we never do. Maybe it’s the source of our neurosis.

The film’s closing shot mirrors that of The Immigrant. Both films are deep meditations on the concept of sacrifice and what that means. In The Immigrant, you get a little bit of uplift because it’s rooted in Ewa’s Catholic faith, and there’s a sense that the sacrifice can have great meaning. But I don’t think Paper Tiger necessarily gives us that same blanket of comfort.

I love your observation. It’s clearly in both movies. There’s no wrong or right, and if that’s what you got out of it, that’s wonderful. I guess I have a little more hope for Irwin than you do. In the end, his business is actually going to take off. He gets that answering machine message. They’ve got a lot of interested businesses, and he has those two children who are going to go off. Yes, they’ll have to endure some terrible stuff, but you know what? Somehow, they’re going to find the power to go on. One of the kids became a wonderful physician. Another one of those kids became a movie director. They’ll be okay. Life goes on. I think Gary’s sacrifice in the film allows Irwin and those two kids to move ahead. That’s actually a pretty big deal.
Interestingly, this is the second interview in a week where a director has mentioned that I’ve had a more pessimistic reading of the ending!
[laughs] Now, why do you think that is, that you have this deep pessimism?

I normally think of myself as an optimistic person, or at least as someone who sees the hopefulness. This isn’t to say I read the film as grim, but here’s another example. As I was watching the film a second time, I thought about the term “paper tiger.” Gary says the Russians are paper tigers who only care about money, and it’s meant as reassurance. And I’m thinking from my perspective today, “What could be more terrifying than if money is all there is?” That’s not reassuring to me. I don’t know if that’s connected at all to my reading of the ending!

No, you’re right. But Gary himself is kind of a paper tiger. He presents himself as the master of two worlds and winds up being a master of none. He says they’re paper tigers, but talk about ironic—that’s a different form of irony. What that means is that they’re not. They’re a malevolent force that’s going to swallow them up. These things are all concurrent, but it doesn’t mean they’re wrong. It just invites multiple interpretations. But that’s actually, I think, a good thing.
